strengths: Addresses an important and practical challenge in 3D avatar creation: enabling a single feed-forward model to handle variable-length inputs (from 1 to many frames) and perform incremental reconstruction without needing per-identity optimization.

The proposed architecture (LGRT), which interleaves frame and global attention while conditioning on head pose, camera parameters, and expression coefficients, is well-motivated and technically sound for aligning dynamic multi-frame facial observations.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation comparing against both optimization-based methods (MonoGaussianAvatar, GaussianAvatars) and feed-forward methods (LAM), demonstrating competitive visual fidelity, cross-view consistency, and fast reconstruction times.
Thorough ablation studies that effectively demonstrate the necessity of each component, including the sliced fusion loss, landmark tracking loss, global attention, and Gaussian pruning mechanism.
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on FLAME tracking for camera poses, head poses, and expression coefficients during both training and inference. While the authors evaluate robustness against landmark noise in Table 4, FLAME fitting itself often requires multi-view optimization or off-the-shelf trackers that take non-negligible time, which is not fully factored into the reported modeling runtime.

Comparison with feed-forward multi-view baselines is somewhat limited: Avat3r Kirschstein et al. (2025) is only compared qualitatively on a few crops from their paper without quantitative benchmark metrics due to lack of public code.

The Gaussian fusion mechanism (Eq. 3) fundamentally concatenates per-frame predicted 3D Gaussians before applying learned pruning. While effective in practice when supervised by the sliced fusion loss, it is relatively simple and causes primitive counts to scale with input frames before pruning.
Minor presentation typos exist (e.g., 'MonoGaussianAvata' in the first sub-table of Table 1).

strengths: The paper addresses a significant and practical limitation in feed-forward 3D avatar generation: bridging the gap between single/fixed-frame feed-forward models and slow optimization-based approaches by supporting arbitrary and variable numbers of input frames.

The integration of alternating frame-level and global attention (inspired by VGGT) with FLAME positional prompts and expression/pose conditioning provides a coherent feed-forward pipeline for animatable 3D Gaussian Splatting.
The use of token compression (FramePack adaptation) to scale the transformer context to hundreds of video frames without running out of GPU memory is an effective design choice.
Comprehensive qualitative and quantitative ablations are provided to justify individual architectural choices, including the global attention, tracking loss, and sliced fusion loss.
weaknesses: Fairness of baseline comparisons: The multi-view evaluation against LAM relies on an ad-hoc modification ('LAM*') to aggregate frames, which was neither trained nor architecturally intended for multi-frame inputs. Consequently, LAM*'s degradation with more views is an expected artifact of an unnatural extension rather than a solid baseline comparison. Similarly, comparing optimization-based methods (MonoGaussianAvatar, GaussianAvatars) on 1 to 4 frames tests them far outside their intended operating regime (minutes of dynamic multi-view video).

Absolute reconstruction fidelity and metrics: The reported PSNR values on NeRSemble remain quite low (around 20–22 dB), which is considerably below the fidelity typically reported by state-of-the-art per-scene avatar reconstruction methods (>28–32 dB). While feed-forward models exhibit some smoothing, a deeper discussion and comparison on novel view and expression synthesis quality against standard avatar benchmarks are lacking.

Limited conceptual novelty: The core model largely synthesizes existing building blocks from recent literature—interleaved attention from VGGT, canonical LBS-based 3DGS prediction from LAM, token compression from FramePack, and mask-based pruning from LP-3DGS/MaskGaussian. The technical novelty primarily resides in assembly and parameter tuning rather than fundamental new representations.

Computational scaling and latency: Reconstruction time scales from 1.33 seconds at 1 view up to 26.06 seconds at 16 views, and even higher for hundreds of frames. This diminishes the claimed feed-forward 'instant/ultra-fast' advantage over lightweight optimization approaches when higher fidelity is desired.

Presentation and writing polish: The abstract ends abruptly with an incomplete sentence ('Code and models are available at '), and several mathematical symbols lack consistent notation between the text and formulation (e.g., superscript vs. subscript indexing for pose/expression latents in Equations 1 and 2).

strengths: Addresses an important and practical limitation in existing feed-forward 3D head avatar reconstruction: the inability of prior models (e.g., LAM, Avat3r) to handle variable-length observation data flexibly and incrementally.

Well-motivated architecture combining alternating frame and global attention with FLAME parametric priors (expression, head pose, and vertex positional prompts), which effectively stabilizes cross-view registration.
Thoughtful training strategies, notably the sliced fusion loss and landmark tracking loss, which prevent ghosting and misalignment when aggregating per-frame Gaussian representations.

Comprehensive experimental results showing consistent quantitative and qualitative scaling in reconstruction quality as the number of available observation frames increases from 1 to 16, as well as an extension to handle longer sequences via token compression.
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on FLAME tracking accuracy: While Table 4 demonstrates tolerance to moderate landmark noise, the framework still fundamentally requires accurate FLAME fits (camera pose, expression, head pose) as inputs; failure in upstream tracking on in-the-wild video directly impacts avatar fidelity.

Fairness of multi-view baselines: In Table 1, LAM was designed strictly for single images; the authors' ad-hoc extension (LAM*) is not trained for multi-view fusion, making its degradation expected. Comparing quantitatively against recent generalizable few-view head avatar baselines (e.g., GPAvatar, HeadGAP, or Avat3r) on a standard benchmark benchmark would provide a more rigorous baseline comparison.

Scalability of rendering speed: As shown in Table 1 and Table 2, despite the Gumbel-Softmax pruning mechanism, the number of Gaussian primitives grows from ~13K (1 view) to ~139K (16 views), resulting in inference rendering speed dropping from 240.17 FPS down to 17.65 FPS. The practical implications of this inference latency degradation should be more thoroughly discussed.

Evaluation diversity: The quantitative evaluation is largely focused on the NeRSemble dataset. Additional comprehensive quantitative cross-dataset evaluations (e.g., on Ava256 or in-the-wild video benchmarks) would significantly bolster the generalizability claims.
